title: The Last Stretch Is a Design-Technology Problem
subtitle: What it takes to hold consumer craft when assistants are writing the first draft

cv.label: Download CV (PDF)
cv.note: Tailored for the Director UX Design role

bio.short: I lead design functions, and the last year went into the layer underneath the craft. UI quality across four platforms, held by a build that refuses work which has left the system.
bio.long:
I lead design functions. The last year went into the layer underneath the craft rather than the craft itself, on purpose. At Bibel TV I own UI quality across iOS, Android, web and connected TV. I prototype in real code against real production APIs rather than in specs, and engineering ships from that code. Engineering there is an external agency, so that workflow crosses a company boundary and holds anyway. Here is the thing I would want to argue about. The hard part of a consumer experience has always been the last stretch, and the last stretch has quietly changed hands. The first draft is written by an assistant now, and what it produces compiles, renders, and looks fine. It is also quietly off-system. So I built the layer that refuses it. Six checks run identically on a laptop and in CI. Two were written against mistakes I watched an AI assistant make: a token reference that does not resolve, and a color hardcoded into a component. Neither shows up as a visual difference, so the build is the only place they surface.

Underneath sits the token architecture. Four tiers, one commit reaching every platform. Alongside it, a color engine where k-means clustering runs in OKLCH rather than RGB, so artwork-driven themes carry even perceptual weight. WCAG contrast is validated inside the algorithm rather than checked at the end. Before that: design leadership at Ninox, with product held alongside it for four months. Five years leading design at Datameer, for a platform used inside regulated banks. One product delivered across six countries under GDPR and church data-protection law. And ten years mentoring and coaching designers at CareerFoundry, alongside all of it.

context.emphasis: Design technology and AI-native practice first, because those are the posting's two most specific bullets and his most differentiated ground. The posting's own last-stretch framing is the hook, and he can answer it with an artifact rather than an opinion. Then craft, then team leadership and critique, then multi-market delivery. The posting explicitly asks for a point of view on scaling AI responsibly. A CV carries evidence, not a point of view, which is what the cover letter is for.
